title: Born Again to a Living Hope
summary: Peter greets God's chosen exiles scattered across Asia Minor and praises God for giving them new birth into a living hope through Jesus' resurrection, an inheritance kept safe in heaven. Their present trials refine their faith like gold, and the salvation they now receive was searched for by the prophets. So they must set their hope on Christ's return, be holy as God is holy, live in reverent fear as those redeemed by Christ's precious blood, and love one another deeply as people born again through God's enduring word.
story: First Peter picks up the story of the church after Pentecost, when the good news had spread far beyond Jerusalem into the provinces of the Roman world. Peter, the fisherman whom Jesus called, who denied him and was restored, and who preached at Pentecost, now writes to believers he may never have met, mostly Gentile converts in Asia Minor. The chapter reaches back to the prophets who foretold Christ's sufferings, to the Passover lamb and the exodus, and to God's command to Israel to be holy, and it reaches forward to the revelation of Jesus Christ at the end of history. The readers are placed between those two points, living the middle of the story with hope.
historical:
The five regions named in verse 1 (Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia) were Roman provinces or districts in Asia Minor, covering most of modern Turkey north of the Taurus mountains, a vast area of cities, towns, and farmland. Some of these churches may have begun through Paul's work in Galatia and Asia (Acts 13-19), while others, in Pontus, Cappadocia, and Bithynia, have no recorded founding; Acts 2:9 mentions visitors from Cappadocia, Pontus, and Asia at Pentecost, and Acts 16:7 says the Spirit prevented Paul from entering Bithynia. How the gospel reached these regions is not known.

The letter's date and authorship are debated (see the introduction). If it comes from Peter, it was written from Rome in the early 60s AD, before his death under Nero. The readers were not facing an empire-wide persecution but the social hostility and local mistreatment that came from abandoning the religious and social life of their towns. Peter's description of their former way of life as empty and inherited from their forefathers (verse 18) suggests that most were Gentiles.
cultural:
Peter calls his readers “exiles of the Dispersion”. The Dispersion was the term for Jews living outside the land of Israel, and exile recalled Israel's captivity in Babylon. Applying these terms to Gentile believers told them that their social displacement was not an accident but part of belonging to God's people, whose true home lay elsewhere. The word behind “your stay as foreigners” in verse 17 (paroikia) described the status of resident aliens, people who lived in a place without full rights of citizenship, a status many in Asia Minor would have known.

The language of redemption in verses 18-19 would resonate in two worlds. For readers who knew the Old Testament, it recalled God's redemption of Israel from Egypt and the Passover lamb, which had to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5). For readers from the Greco-Roman world, redemption meant the payment of a price to free a slave or captive, and they would know that silver and gold were the ordinary currency of such a purchase. Gold was refined by fire to remove impurities, an image used in the Old Testament for God's testing of his people (Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3).
literary: The letter opens in the standard form of an ancient letter (sender, recipients, greeting), expanded with a Trinitarian description of the readers' election by the Father, sanctification by the Spirit, and sprinkling by Christ's blood. Verses 3-12 are a single outpouring of praise, written in Greek as long, flowing sentences, beginning with “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ”, a form of Jewish blessing adapted to Christ. The praise then turns to exhortation with “Therefore” in verse 13, and the commands of verses 13-25 grow directly from what God has done: because God has given new birth, set your hope; because he is holy, be holy; because you were redeemed at great cost, live in reverent fear; because you were born again, love one another. The chapter ends with a quotation from Isaiah 40:6-8, contrasting fading human glory with the enduring word of the Lord.

outline.t: Praise for new birth into a living hope
The salvation the prophets searched for
Redeemed by the precious blood of Christ
Love one another, born of the enduring word

doctrines.note: Salvation is past, present, and future: believers have been given new birth and redeemed, they are now “receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls”, and they await the salvation “ready to be revealed in the last time.”

Verse 2 names the Father's foreknowledge, the Spirit's sanctifying work, and obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by his blood, a pattern that shows the three persons working together in salvation, which the church later confessed as the Trinity.
“Be holy, because I am holy” (quoting Leviticus). Holiness flows from God's character and from his calling, and it means a life no longer shaped by former passions but set apart for God.

Hope is “living” because it rests on the resurrection of Jesus and looks to an inheritance that is “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading.” Believers are to set their hope fully on the grace to be given at Christ's revelation.

words.note: Anagennaō, to give new birth or cause to be born again. The word appears in the New Testament only here (verses 3 and 23). It describes salvation as God's act of giving life, not a human achievement, and it echoes Jesus' teaching that a person must be born again (John 3:3).

Parepidēmos, a sojourner or temporary resident, someone living away from home. Abraham used a related term of himself among the Hittites (Genesis 23:4 in the Greek Old Testament). Peter uses it for believers who belong to God's people and whose true home is not where they now live.

Elpis, hope. In the New Testament hope is confident expectation of what God has promised, not uncertain wishing. Peter calls it a living hope grounded in the resurrection, and in verse 21 says believers' faith and hope are in God.

Lutroō, to redeem or ransom, to free by paying a price. Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with Christ's precious blood, recalling both Israel's redemption from Egypt and Jesus' saying that he came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

christ: Christ fills this chapter. His resurrection is the source of the believer's new birth and living hope. His coming revelation is the goal toward which the whole Christian life is directed. He is loved though unseen, which is striking from Peter, who had seen him. He is “a lamb without blemish or spot”, whose precious blood redeems, recalling the Passover lamb and the servant of Isaiah 53. He was “known before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in the last times”, so his coming was God's plan from the beginning, not an afterthought. And the prophets themselves, moved by “the Spirit of Christ”, spoke of his sufferings and the glories that would follow, the pattern that the rest of the letter applies to his people.

hard.q: What does it mean to be chosen “according to the foreknowledge of God the Father”?
hard.a: Peter calls his readers the elect, chosen according to God's foreknowledge. Christians agree that salvation begins with God's gracious initiative, but they understand election in different ways. In the Reformed or Calvinist tradition, foreknowledge here means more than knowing facts in advance; it is God's prior loving commitment to his people, as the same word is used of Christ in verse 20, and election is God's sovereign choice of particular persons for salvation. In the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, God chooses those whom he foreknows will respond in faith, and his grace enables but does not compel that response. Others emphasize that election in Scripture is often corporate: God chooses a people, now defined as those who are in Christ, as he once chose Israel. All these views affirm that God's choice is gracious, that it gives assurance to believers under pressure, and that it leads to obedience (verse 2 speaks of being chosen “for obedience”). Peter's pastoral purpose is clear: people who have lost their place in society are reminded that God has chosen them.

questions: Peter calls his readers exiles and foreigners. In what ways do you feel out of place because of your faith, and how does his description of a living hope speak to that?
Verse 7 describes trials as refining faith like gold. How has a hard season revealed or strengthened what you truly trust?
Peter grounds his call to holiness and love in what God has already done. Why does the order matter, and how might it change the way you approach obedience?
